en: The *Dāṭhāvaṃsa*:
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One,
who is confident in the path of discourse.
I pay homage to the Teacher, whose range is infinite,
who has conquered the invincible light that illuminates the three worlds,
and who has abandoned every veil of the knowable.
Born from the Lord of the World, dispelling fear,
practiced by those of pure knowledge and conduct,
it cuts through the fetters and bonds of proliferation.
I pay homage to the Dhamma, subtle and very difficult to see,
wherein even by a mere gladdening of heart,
living beings touch the deathless state, the destruction of suffering.
I bow to that Saṅgha, worthy of offerings, whose faculties are well-composed, the disciples of the King of Sages;
who, like a black cobra, possesses natural brilliance.
Parakkama, the compassionate commander-in-chief,
who sought the growth and welfare of the people while searching for the teaching of the Conqueror.
Born of the pure Paṇḍu lineage, whose radiance was like the stainless moon,
possessing well-grown faith in the teaching of the King of Sages,
she spoke kindly and followed the path of moral conduct.
Always mindful, like a mother to her child, the chief queen—
endowed with the wealth of great majesty and a lofty mind— was dear to the king who enjoyed his valorous achievements.
Having appointed Līlāvatī as the sovereign who grants all desired objects and protects the entire surface of Laṅkā, he [appointed] the prince,
whose virtuous ministers were well-honored.
Having established the Greatly Compassionate one,
born of the lineage of wise lords, named Madhurinda,
who was well-trained in the sacred word and in the arts.
Having long dispelled the infamy of the "Three Lions" that had persisted for a very long time among the people,
he [honored] them for a long time with excellent robes and other requisites.
He satisfied those who were well-restrained and self-controlled.
Desiring the long endurance of the teaching,
the grateful one, endowed with wisdom, exerted his prowess.
I was requested with great reverence by the wise Candimabandhu Kittisiri,
who, together with Sinhalese poets, [composed] in the language of his own country.
I shall compose this chronicle of the tooth-relic of the Victor,
for the growth of the Māgadhī language,
even for those dwelling in other islands.
This Victor, having once lived in the city called Amaravati during the Age of Plenty,
was known by the name Sumedha, being an expert in the analysis of all the Vedas and their auxiliary branches.
In a wealthy and prosperous family, I was a young man.
For I am oppressed by the ruin of my birth,
overcome by old age, and overwhelmed by death.
Thinking to himself in solitude, "I shall seek the auspicious state free from birth, old age,
and the rest," he [considered] his countless wealth and abundance of grain.
Having established [the Dhamma] among the poor—
though it is difficult to give— it, leaving behind friends, sons, and kinsmen who were bound to him by no small weight of affection.
Having abandoned all delightful sensual pleasures,
he went forth from his home to the vicinity of the Himālaya mountains,
to the mountain renowned as Dhammika.
Having entered with equanimity that hermitage— adorned with rows of various trees,
pleasing to the mind, fashioned by the king of the gods,
and inaccessible to those who have not attained the goal.
Turning back his hair, wearing a deerskin,
he took up the guise of an ascetic with matted locks; well-restrained,
with senses fully subdued, he was surrounded by a retinue.
Sustaining his body with various fruits and such,
he reached mastery over the higher knowledges (abhiññā);
there he experienced the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti).
Adorned by the joyful populace dwelling in the delightful city,
he proceeded directly toward the place on the path where he was to alight.
While his task was still unaccomplished, O wise one, the ascetic [approached] the Leader,
the destroyer of existence, the one who seeks Nibbāna,
who perceives the further shore of the unfathomable ocean of those to be known.
He once beheld the Buddha Dīpaṅkara,
who was attended by many lakhs of those whose taints were destroyed;
then, [he saw] the Lord of the Three Worlds together with his Saṅgha.
Having sacrificed even his own body and life,
having cast aside his matted hair, antelope skin, and other accoutrements,
he constructed a bridge for his very self across the shallow pool.
"O Greatly Compassionate One, without stepping upon the mud,
let him go on my back together with his monks";
having thus resolved, he lay down there.
Having observed these three realms of existence as being without a protector,
my mind is impelled by compassion to rescue people who are afflicted by suffering within the ocean of worldly existence.
He made a great resolve with exalted effort for the attainment of the state of perfect enlightenment; and then,
having understood his intention, [the Buddha] who is master of himself—
The Great Sage gave him a prophecy; then,
after the Tathāgata had departed from that city, he,
dwelling in solitude, contemplated the qualities of the perfections.
And thereafter, for four hundred thousand incalculable aeons, his prowess remained unstained;
throughout various births, he cultivated the perfections leading to enlightenment.
He fulfilled the qualities of pure accumulations;
then, of great renown, he was reborn in Tusita for the sake of attaining the state of pure enlightenment.
Waiting for the opportune moment,
the one whose wealth is compassion experienced sovereignty in every way for a long time throughout the ten thousand world-systems.
Having approached with great joy for the sake of attaining victory over the Māras,
he was respectfully entreated by many gathered lords of the gods and others.
Then, having passed away from there,
he was born in the city of Kapilavatthu as the preeminent banner of the Śākya clan, ever mindful, under King Suddhodana.
The son of the great queen Mahāmāyā,
as soon as he was born from the earth,
stood up and gazed toward the quarters.
Then the quarters with their peaks uncovered became visible,
and there gods and humans paid him honor,
holding up sunshades and other such offerings.
Remaining invisible in the sky, the deity approached him from the north and,
facing northward, uttered these seven words in a voice like that of a bull.
Named Kumāra because his name was established according to reality,
possessing great strength and a body that captivated with youth, he—
among those three [seasons] appropriate for the three times of day— [remained] in the three [seasons] suitable for the three watches of the night.
You have experienced prosperity within the finest palaces;
yet at times, along the garden paths, you have seen one struck by old age,
one thus afflicted by illness, and one who has passed away— O self-controlled one!
Gradually, having seen through this, his mind became dispassionate;
he desired to go forth from the world, abandoning all states of existence.
At night, with offerings of flowers, lamps, and the like, he prepared for his departure.
Honored by those who dwell in the three heavens,
the Great Compassionate One, having mounted his well-harnessed horse Kanthaka, went forth from there.
Having gradually reached the peerless river Āpagā,
whose banks were sprinkled with water from pearls as bright as polished gems,
he stood there, adorned with a noble crown of flowers.
He tossed it up into the sky like a white cloth.
Then the Lord of the Thirty-three, having received it with his excellent golden casket, [placed it therein].
In his former life, he had a cetiya made of sapphires three yojanas in size, with a crest-jewel (*cūḷāmaṇi*) for himself.
Then, by Ghaṭīkāra and Sajoṇi...
He took up the robes and other requisites that had been brought together,
and then, having assumed a most excellent form,
he cast his own pair of garments into the expanse of the sky.
Having accepted it, the one of great psychic power, seated upon his lotus throne and impelled by a weight of devotion,
fashioned a celestial mansion twelve yojanas in extent within his own realm.
The cloth stupa with blue and other gems:
one whose self is well-restrained, mindful, with senses conquered,
modest in appearance, and free from taste and greed;
With extraordinary stride, he exerted himself for six years in the Great Struggle, which was so difficult to perform.
On the full moon day of the month of Visākha—
With equanimity as the root of his co-nascent enlightenment,
he resolved upon a grass seat measuring fourteen cubits and sat down with energy.
Covering the earth and the sky,
terrifying with his assumption of hideous forms,
he caused the great earth together with its mountains to tremble.
The Victor conquered the army of Māra in the evening.
When the three worlds were adorned with flower-made arches and other decorations by hosts of gods, asuras, and brahmās;
While the sound of the divine drums was resounding,
at the end of the night he awakened to enlightenment;
then the earth, with its mountains and forests, trembled.
He agitated ten thousand world-systems, as vast as the salt ocean,
and a great radiance spread throughout the worlds.
The blind regained their stainless eyes;
even those born deaf heard sounds;
and the mute spoke with melodious speech.
The lame walked on foot through the mud;
those with straight and graceful bodies became hunchbacked;
and even Sikhī attained parinibbāna in the Avīci hell and other realms.
Sentient beings were released from their bonds;
the state of being a peta, with its hunger and other afflictions, departed.
The diseases and calamities of living beings subsided.
Fear did not oppress those born as animals;
people were friendly and spoke kindly,
and the elephants let out their trumpet-like cries.
The horses neighed with joyful minds,
all the drums resounded of their own accord,
and the ornaments on the bodies of living beings rang out.
The quarters became serene on every side.
A gentle, cool, and pleasant breeze blew,
and even a cloud rained down out of season.
Birds flew through the sky,
the earth burst forth with water,
and rivers stood still as if they were not flowing.
In the sky, all the lights shone forth;
states of existence became manifest on every side,
and there was no need for people to utter words.
Mountains and other such things were no longer obstructive to one another's view;
even the fragrance considered divine was wafted abroad;
and the trees became laden with fruits and flowers.
The lake was covered with lotuses;
on both dry land and in the water,
flowers of every kind bloomed and blossomed in all their variety.
With a continuous rain of fragrant flowers,
the entire earth and sky became covered;
there, the Victor sat upon an excellent couch.
Experiencing the bliss born of dwelling in meditative attainment,
he passed seven days while enjoying that which he had long desired.
Then, having ascended into the courtyard of the sky,
the Great Sage displayed a pair of miracles,
together with a display of supernormal power, for the inhabitants of the triple heaven.
He dispelled the doubt regarding the victory.
Then, having descended from the seat of victory,
he stood leaning against the eastern and northern corners.
With eyes that blinked not for seven days,
he worshipped that seat and the Bodhi tree; then,
on the jeweled walkway in the intermediate space, the Victor—
Of the standing place and of the seat,
both magnificent and fashioned by the best of gods,
he made seven crooks.
Then, having entered another Bodhi tree at the Abode of Jewels,
the Victor contemplated the method of the *Samantapāṭhāna*.
Seven days passed in this manner. Then,
a stream of radiance, free from all obstruction,
issued forth from the Teacher’s body.
And it spread everywhere— above, below, and all around— through world-systems empty of measure.
At the foot of the banyan tree, they were perceived as goat-herders.
Experiencing the bliss born of seclusion,
the Leader, Anantadassī, who is honored by the king of the gods, dwelt for seven days.
He dwelt at the foot of the Mucalinda tree,
seated within the hollow of the coils of the serpent Mucalinda,
upon a bed strewn with flowers.
The Conqueror spent seven days in meditation at Vāsava;
the Sage also dwelt for seven days and nights in meditation at the Rājāyatana tree.
Then the Thousand-Eyed One gave tooth-sticks and mouth-rinsing water to the Teacher.
Thereafter, [he offered] that which had been brought by the most excellent great kings.
Having fashioned a bowl made of stone, either square or single,
and having placed therein a lump of honey as its base,
he accepted it after it had been brought by a merchant.
Having performed his duty and established both Tapassu and Bhallika in the refuges,
he gave them of his own accord to honor them.
Having touched his head with its hair at the foot of the banyan tree,
he was entreated by Sahampati Brahmā,
who perceived him as the keeper of goats.
To perform a supreme gathering of the Dhamma for the sake of the people,
the Sage went alone to Bārāṇasī.
Having gone to the Deer Park at Isipatana, the abode of the self-restrained, that King of Dhamma—
Seated there upon his throne, in that place rendered immovable,
on the full moon day of Āsāḷha when the world-system was illuminated by the radiance of the moon’s light,
he turned the Wheel of Dhamma, which removes the stains of evil from the gods, Brahmas, and others.
Having heard that True Dhamma-path, which spreads throughout the expanse of the hollows of the three worlds,
eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, headed by the sage Koṇḍañña of the twice-born clan who attained final knowledge,
realized the Dhamma of the Path within this Cakkavāḷa, which is otherwise so limited and devoid of such beings; it was a sublime occurrence.
A radiance appeared, and immediately there were many kinds of wonders.
This was the first chapter.
From that time forth, that Teacher began training gods and humans.
In the month of Phussa, on the ninth full-moon day after his enlightenment,
having come to Laṅkā, he stayed at the Mahānāgavana garden on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
which was one yojana wide and three yojanas in length.
Having gone to the assembly of the yakkhas and standing there in the sky,
he caused the yakkhas to be struck with fear by means of wind, darkness,
and rain. When those yakkhas had obtained safety, he was given land by them.
Having spread out a piece of leather and sat down at that very moment,
he increased it by means of his supernormal power until it extended all around as far as the Indus River; the piece of leather was ablaze with fire, filled with garlands of flames.
With speed, when the night-stalker had become a mass at the edge of the ocean,
the Victor brought him to this island of Giri and established him there. Then, having taught the Dhamma in that assembly of gods, he—
On Mount Sumanakūṭaka, he brought about the realization of the Dhamma for many millions of beings.
Having given his hair so that the god Mahāsumana might pay homage to it, the Jina went to Jetavana.
Having established them upon the ground where the Teacher’s seat had been,
he constructed a stupa made of sapphire and paid it honor.
Relying upon his jeweled couch, he dwelt amidst the mountains and forests.
Having seen the two Nāgas, Cūḷodara and Mahodara, seeking battle,
the Great Sage went to Nāgadīpa on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight in the month of Citta, in the fifth year after his Enlightenment.
Then the god Samiddhisumana, his mind filled with joy, took up the Rājāyatana tree standing in the Jeta Grove— his own very abode—
as if it were a peak of sapphire, and departed with a delighted heart.
Having taken it and made it a parasol for the Teacher,
he went along with him. While the great battle between the two nāga kings was underway,
the Protector, seated in the sky, caused a great darkness to be produced.
Then, having shown the light and comforted the wealthy ones,
the Bull among Men spoke the Dhamma that brings about harmony.
There were eighty koṭis of nāgas dwelling in the immovable oceans.
The joyful serpent-lords established themselves in the precepts and the refuges.
Having offered a jeweled couch to the Teacher,
they gratified the Great Hero, seated thereon, with food and drink.
Having established the Rājāyatana tree there,
he gave that throne to the Nāgas for their worship.
In the eighth year after the Enlightenment, on the full moon day of Vesākha—
Invited by the lord of nāgas named Maṇiakkhika,
he went to the well-prepared palace of that very nāga king,
accompanied by five hundred monks from Kalyāṇī.
In the jewel pavilion constructed at the site of the Kalyāṇī Cetiya,
the Bull among Men sat upon a most noble couch.
With celestial foods, both hard and soft, he [honored] the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha.
Honored by the serpents, that Lord of Serpents gladdened them.
Having taught the True Dhamma, which brings about the happiness of heaven and liberation,
the Teacher left a footprint-mark upon Mount Sumana.
Then, at the foot of the mountain, that Leader together with his Saṅgha,
having spent the day’s rest, approached Dīghavāpī. There,
at the site of the stupa, the Buddha together with his Saṅgha sat down.
He experienced incomparable bliss arising from meditative attainment.
At the site of the Mahābodhi tree, the Victor established himself in concentration;
and at the location of the Mahāthūpa, he dwelt in concentration.
In the vicinity of the Thūpārāma, at the site of the stupa, the Fully Enlightened One,
together with the community of monks, spent a short while in the bliss of meditative absorption.
Standing in the area of the Stone Stupa, the Sage, who was not ignorant of the proper time, remained there.
Having instructed him thus, he then went to Jetavana.
Free from greed for gain and honor, enduring with equanimity even unbearable insults,
he did so solely out of a desire to deliver the entire world.
Having remained for forty-five years,
and having taught the ninefold dispensation of the Teacher consisting of the Suttas and so forth,
he delivered across the wilderness of existence those people who were beyond counting.
Having completed all the duties of a Buddha, the Visionary,
in the city of Kusinārā, in the grove of the Malla kings,
within the Sāl forest between the twin Sāla trees, [passed away].
On the full moon day of Vesākha, lying on his right side in the lion’s posture upon a costly, well-prepared couch with its head toward the north,
he taught the supreme Dhamma to the Mallas during the first watch of the night.
Having brought Subhadda to the deathless state during the middle watch,
the Bhikkhu, during the final watch, having compiled the entire mass of Dhamma and exhorted them with the theme of heedfulness.
At the time of dawn, rising from his dwelling in the attainment of jhāna, he attained final nibbāna,
free from all remaining substrate. Then there were earthquakes and other wonders that brought amazement.
Many offerings were made by numerous gods and humans.
However, those desiring to understand the specific details of the offerings in their entirety,
they should be known according to the sequence stated in the *Parinibbāna Sutta*.
Having first wrapped the Victor with unwashed cloths,
and having wrapped him with finely combed cotton wool,
she carefully wrapped him thus five hundred times.
Having placed [the body] in a golden trough filled with oil,
the leaders of the Mallas then erected a funeral pyre constructed from fragrant wood, rising to a height of one hundred and twenty cubits.
When the Elder Mahākassapa had not yet paid homage to the King of Dhamma,
the funeral pyre did not ignite due to the power of the gods' resolve.
Thereupon, the leaders of the Malla kings exerted themselves in many ways.
They were unable to cause that funeral pyre, the consumer of oblations,
to accept the robes and other items, the great wooden trough, and the highly precious pyre itself, because of the resolve made by the Elder Mahākassapa.
Having divided herself in two and emerged, she established herself upon her own head;
having paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, she remained established in her original place.
Then, through the power of the gods, the funeral pyre burst into flames.
There was neither ash nor charcoal from the Teacher’s body when it was cremated;
only his relics remained, radiant like pearls and glowing with the luster of gold,
scattered in many ways because no one was present to behold the Buddha.
The cranial bone, the two collarbones, and the four canine teeth—
these seven relics were not scattered by the Teacher.
Even though they fell from the sky or rose up from the surface of the earth, [they remained together].
From all sides, streams of water extinguished the fire of the funeral pyre.
This was the elder named Sarabhū, a great disciple of the elder Sāriputta, possessed of great supernormal power and having attained the analytical knowledges.
Having taken the neck-relic from the citadel and established it upon the Great Stupa in the Mahiyangana courtyard, he constructed the Kancuka Cetiya.
This compassionate sage named Khema, whose fetters were exhausted, [performed this deed].
Then Doṇa, the most excellent of the twice-born,
having resolved the conflict that had arisen among the eight kings for the sake of the Teacher’s relics,
took the left canine tooth relic from the funeral pyre.
Having divided the remaining relics into eight portions,
he gave them to the eighteen kings who dwelt in various cities.
Having received those relics, those lords of men were joyful and delighted.
Having returned to their respective kingdoms, they had cetiyas constructed.
One tooth was honored by the Lord of the Gods (Indra),
one by the inhabitants of Gandhāra, and one by the kings of the nāgas.
Then Khema gave the tooth-relic that he himself had received to King Brahmadatta of Kaliṅga in Dantapura.
Having taught the Dhamma and shattered all wrong views, he—
He inspired faith in that king regarding the supreme, profound Triple Gem.
Having plunged into the ocean of the nectar of the Dhamma of the Lord of Sages,
that lord of men washed away the impurities of stinginess and the like.
Like a rain-cloud pouring down various jewels,
that Supreme among Men extinguished the scorching heat of poverty.
It was adorned with hanging tassels inlaid with gold and networks of pearls.
Covered with hundreds of gabled pavilions, resembling the rising sun,
difficult to behold due to the splendor of various jewels, captivating to the eye,
this vehicle brings about the attainment of heaven and the supreme state of liberation through its extraordinary grace.
Having had a temple for the tooth-relic constructed,
and having likewise had a relic throne made there, resplendent with jewels,
the king placed the tooth-relic of the Great Sage within it.
He worshipped with objects of veneration day and night without weariness.
Thus, having accumulated a perfect store of merit,
he cast off his human body and adorned the celestial realm.
Then his son, known as the King of Kāsi, was born after him;
having obtained the kingdom, he dispelled the sting of sorrow for his ministers.
Having honored that tooth-relic with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, [he paid homage].
He caused the relic shrine to be illuminated constantly with jewel-lamps.
Having thus accumulated a store of merit, the king,
upon casting off his own body, attained the city of the Lord of Devas.
There was a lord of kings named Sunanda, who brought joy to the virtuous;
from him was born a son, a devotee of the Buddha’s teaching.
Having honored the Tooth Relic of the Knower of All That Is to Be Known, he—
With great devotion, he went to the company of the gods.
After him, many other lords of the earth also successively paid homage to the Tooth Relic of the Lord of Sages.
The king named Guhasīva, whose command was difficult to transgress,
having attained the glory of sovereignty, protected the great masses of people.
Yet he [was] greedy for gain and honor, ignorant of his own and others' welfare.
He approached the deceitful Nigaṇṭhas who were blinded by ignorance.
Like the moon shrouded by a mass of mist during the rainy season,
that Bull among Men was unable to shine with the rays of his virtues.
Even though these followers of the path of Dhamma had entered the forest of views,
other living beings could not overtake that excellent path,
which was adorned with golden gateways, garlands, banners, and plantain trees.
Having adorned the city with many flower garlands,
the citizens decorated it with the sounds of auspicious hymns, dancing, singing, and the like,
as well as with flowers of gold and silver, perfumes, aromatic powders, and other offerings.
While worshipping the tooth-relic of the King of Sages at that time,
they raised a single roar resembling the crashing of the ocean at the end of an aeon.
Then the lord of men opened the lion-window of the palace.
As he was walking along, the king saw the people intent on the ritual of worship.
Then, entering the assembly of ministers with a mind filled with wonder,
agitated by curiosity, he spoke these words:
"What is this wonder? Of what kind is this miracle?
Why is this city of mine filled with festive joy?
Then the wise minister, a devotee of the Buddha, explained:
To that king who did not understand the power of the Fully Enlightened One—
the All-Conquering Buddha who perceives the destruction of craving—
this relic, O Great King, was brought by the Elder Khema.
Having honored that relic here, the kings of old,
relying upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta), attained the company of the gods.
All these citizens as well, seeking the welfare of their future lives, [have done the same].
"Gathering together, they pay homage to that relic of the Teacher.
Having heard these well-spoken words of Dharma from that minister,
the king cast off the stain of his ill-fortune and placed his faith in the Triple Gem.
While performing this worship of the relics, the king brought wonder to the world;
he made the hostile heretics joyful and the other people delighted.
"All these are shameless, devoid of virtues such as faith."
"Stubborn, deceitful, and lacking wisdom, they are obstacles to heaven and liberation.
Having reflected thus, the king of men, Guhasīva,
banished those Nigaṇṭhas from his kingdom without exception.
Then all those Nigaṇṭhas, blazing with the fire of anger like fires sprinkled with ghee,
went to the city of Pāṭaliputta. There,
the king was of great majesty, the lord of Jambudīpa.
At that time, there was one named Paṇḍu, who possessed infinite power and a vast army.
Then the Nigaṇṭhas, driven by anger and all intent on sowing discord,
approached the king and spoke these words.
To you, who possess great psychic power and are worthy of worship by all gods and humans,
Śiva, Brahmā, and the other deities constantly pay homage.
Now, however, even Guhasīva, the neighboring king, pays homage to you.
"Blaming such a god, he pays homage to a mere corpse.
Having heard their words, the king, driven by the power of anger,
then spoke to his general, the vassal ruler Cittayāna:
Having gone to the kingdom of Kaliṅga,
he honored that skeleton in the cave named Sīva for a day and night.
Then King Cittayāna, with his great fourfold army, [departed].
Having stationed his own army, he departed from that place in the past.
Having gone forth, that protector of the earth, preceded by his military divisions,
established his camp not far from Dantapura.
Having heard of his arrival, that king of Kaliṅga gratified the lord of men with the gift of a lordly elephant and other offerings.
Having recognized the king Guhasīva’s intention for his welfare, [he acted accordingly].
Traveling by chariot together with his army, he entered Dantapura. That king beheld the city,
which was adorned with walls, gate-towers, battlements, palaces,
and watchtowers, and made magnificent with halls for the distribution of alms.
Then Sumana, having gone there,
entered the royal palace and delivered the message to King Paṇḍu and Guhasīva.
Having heard that terrible and insurmountable message of his, [he was overcome].
With a serene countenance, Cittayāna spoke thus:
"For the sake of the welfare of the entire world,
having untiringly accumulated vast stores of merit through the giving of flesh, eyes, and other gifts over countless eons."
Having conquered the army of Namuci and attained the destruction of all taints,
he has gone beyond all phenomena through unobstructed knowledge.
Disregarding the enjoyment of his own visible-world happiness, he—
He who, by means of the ship of the Dhamma, ferried people across the ocean of existence—
to that Buddha, the god beyond gods, the refuge of all living beings,
people indeed show contempt; surely they are deceived.
Having heard such words of praise for the Teacher,
King Guhasīva manifested his faith through continuous expressions of joy.
Observing that his mind was thus purified, Guhasīva— whose nature was cool— gazed upon him with serene confidence.
Together with him, he went to that costly relic shrine,
which was fashioned from yellow sandalwood and featured door-frames and other parts made of coral, as well as hanging garlands of pearls.
Adorned with panels of sapphire, with jeweled bells, and with golden ear-ornaments, it was beautified by a jeweled pinnacle.
Its high roof, radiant with beryl, was crowded with sea-monsters.
He beheld the Relic Shrine with its jewel-bright pedestal.
Then, seeing beneath the white sunshade the relic casket adorned with jewels, he was filled with joy and attained a state of wonder.
Then that Lord of Kaliṅga, having opened the casket and placed his right knee upon the surface of the earth,
raised his hands in añjali and [proclaimed] the virtues of the One Possessing Ten Powers and the others.
Having remembered this, he made a formal supplication to the Best of Buddhas:
"At the foot of the Gaṇḍamba tree, while you were subduing the heretics,
you displayed a wondrous miracle of the twin [miracles]."
Having filled the courtyard of the world-system with flames and fires emerging from his front body and other parts, he inspired faith in all people. Then,
for three months, he taught the Abhidhamma, which is like nectar to the wise.
As you descended from Tāvatiṃsa into the city of Saṅkassa,
you were honored in manifold ways by Brahmās, devas, asuras, and others,
who carried your parasol, fan, conch, and other regalia.
Standing upon the jeweled staircase fashioned by Vissakamma,
you displayed the miracle named "The Opening of the World.
Likewise, O King of Sages, on many other occasions, you again—
"Many miracles were displayed by the Self-Existent One.

their hearts were filled with joy at that moment.
While shouts of "Sādhu! and other words of praise spread throughout the boundless sky,
the tooth-relic of the Sugata entered the interior of the jeweled casket.
Then, having descended from the expanse of the sky,
those hosts of hooded serpents obstructed her boat for seven days and nights with a magnificent great makara.
Seeing a celestial mansion like a ship in the sky,
motionless in the midst of a vast ocean of darkness,
those husband and wife, their hearts agitated by fear, together—
They remembered him, the possessor of psychic powers,
the son of the One Endowed with Ten Powers. Immediately perceiving their thoughts,
the Son of the Sage arrived, crushing the rows of clouds in the sky as he went.
Having fashioned a massive body of the Lord of Birds,
he quickly drove away those snakes who were trembling with fear.
Thus, when the two sons of the Buddha had dispelled the terror caused by the serpents and departed,
That ship, its banners fluttering in the wind, shattering the lofty rows of waves with the speed of its course,
suddenly descended upon the city of Laṅkā— which resembled a vast mass of clouds—
by virtue of that Elder’s supernatural power.
The Fourth Chapter.
In the ninth year of the Great King Mahādisa,
[this was written] for the son of King Kittisirimegha.
Then that couple, having descended into that city, dwelt in a delightful temple.
Having seen those two travelers there at night, the excellent brahmin—
He regaled them with sweet foods and drinks;
and at the end of the night, he announced the path to Anurādhapura to those lords of the trees.
Then, having taken that most excellent tooth-relic of the Jina,
they were honored by the best of brahmins and departed from the city;
having set out, they traveled along a very distant road.
They went from Padvāra village to Anurādhapura;
having reflected upon that righteous and excellent man,
the husband and wife arrived at this region.
They heard that the Lord of Laṅkā had passed away long ago due to a great disease that had arisen;
they were overcome with grief as if by a mountain peak rising up.
Overwhelmed, they lamented excessively in their confusion;
then, as their minds were fainting away,
all the cardinal and intermediate directions became thick with darkness.
Having heard that King Kittisirimegha,
while established in sovereignty, held the Triple Gem as his own,
the regions were like forests whose great fires had been extinguished by rain.
Having heard from a certain bhikkhu at the Mahāvihāra named Meghagiri that he was beloved by the king, that husband and wife became free from grief and distress.
Having approached him and performed the rites of hospitality,
the two of them, meeting together, spoke of the manifestation of the relics.
Having heard of the tenfold manifestation, that excellent sage—
With his body anointed as if with the essence of ambrosia,
he immediately increased the stainless relic in his own home,
which was adorned with spread canopies.
Having performed this most excellent service for both that husband and wife according to their wishes,
it is fitting to relate this account in full.
The Lord of Laṅkā dispatched a messenger-monk with a message. One day,
during the spring season, the king was enjoying the pleasure of sporting in the garden together with his beloved women.
Then, even from very far off as he was approaching,
the monk saw him whose facial complexion was serene.
Having approached that lord of men, the self-controlled one—
With a joyful heart, he proclaimed this account;
having heard it, bearing a weight of supreme rapture,
the king became like one who has attained the Wheel-Treasure.
"The supreme brahmin Laṅkissara shall take the tooth-relic of the Victor;
both husband and wife, having come together,
will go to Laṅkā before long"— thus was it proclaimed.
And he considered the words of the soothsayer to be true.
Then the king, together with a great assembly,
[set out] toward that city of Anurādhapura, situated beyond the [other] cities.
With a faithful and serene mind, he immediately went on foot to that monastery, Meghagiri, out of longing for it;
and there he beheld the relics of the Sugata, which are beyond all acquisition.
And with the streams of tears from his eyes like a necklace of bright pearls,
having made a vow preceded by great reverence, he,
wearing a mantle of horripilation, thought thus:
If I were to offer today my own head— the most precious limb so difficult to give—
to the Tathāgata, the sole refuge of the three worlds, who wears a crown resplendent with many jewels, I would do so.
I would not do anything unbecoming to this realm.
Even if one were to worship the entire circle of the earth,
along with its abundant jewels, wealth, and enjoyments;
"Who in the worlds, being free from delusion, would think: 'I shall perform worship befitting that [status]'?
This sovereignty over Laṅkā was but a very small thing for me."
The Buddha is immeasurable due to his manifold qualities;
how then could I, one of such limited fortune, pass away while the Ten-Powered One, the sole protector of the three worlds, still remains?
Thus, reflecting on that very same thing again and again, he—
though endowed with fortitude— fell into a state of unconsciousness,
suddenly fanned by the breeze from the whisks.
The dejected servants received a sign. Then,
even when sowing only a small amount of seed upon a vast expanse of fertile soil,
the wise [reaped a great harvest].
In due season, they receive flowers, fruits,
and other such things in no small measure, obtaining the fruits they have desired.
Thus, you too are immeasurable through your manifold virtues.
Having made even this small offering to the Lord of Dhamma,
through the excellence of its transformation over time,
I shall obtain the peerless happiness of heaven and liberation.
Having reflected thus, with an excess of overflowing joy,
the lord of men, whose face resembled the full moon,
[honored] that All-Knowing One, the supreme among the ten types of relics.
He honored this entire island of Sīhaḷa.
There were also monks who were masters of the Tipiṭaka, reciters of the Jātaka,
and others skilled in logic and other fields, as well as those who were wise and intelligent.
Even the clansmen, who had taken refuge in the single essence of the Triple Gem,
immediately gathered there out of curiosity;
then the king, in the midst of that great assembly, [spoke].
Thus spoke the eminent sage, whose teeth were exceedingly white:
"If the Buddha’s tooth were like the star Osadhi,
why would it appear so dark and dull?"
At that moment, the ten-fold power of the Sage,
the Lord of Men, was spread abroad through the courtyard of the sky like two royal swans who have outstretched their wings.
In an instant, with the speed of a flash,
he spread a priceless rug over the ground and placed the relics of the Lord of Sages upon a magnificent throne.
The king closed it with a covering of jasmine flowers,
which possessed a luster equal to the peak of Mount Meru at the end of the rains.
Then, the relic of the Lord of Sages quickly emerged.
Standing upon the summit of that heap of flowers,
she shone with rays white as milk,
causing those who beheld her to gaze with unblinking eyes.
Having placed that relic upon a throne,
he covered it with hundreds of costly garments and fine cloths resembling a film on milk-ocean water.
Furthermore, out of a desire to investigate further,
he suddenly burst through hundreds of garments,
like the moon emerging from the belly of a white cloud.
Standing above them, she illuminated all directions with rays as pure as jasmine;
at that moment, the earth together with its mountains was bathed in light.
As if emitting the cry of "Excellent!
in response, the ocean gazed at that marvel as if it were something unprecedented;
its arms of waves became motionless and utterly still.
Even from the *supupa* and *sāla* trees shaken by intoxicated elephants, celestial flowers fell from the sky;
and the people marveled at the extraordinary grace of the dancing.
The celestial beauties also displayed themselves in the sky;
even the singers seated upon their thrones sang songs,
delightful with the loud, joyful clamor born of their ecstasy.
They also played divine musical instruments, which produced a deep,
loud, and sweet sound, doubled in resonance;
interwoven like a hundred fine threads of silver rope.
With hundreds of torrents from the cloud that fills both earth and sky,
all directions were filled with the great roar of thundering clouds,
while hundreds of lamps in the form of the rays of brilliant lightning illuminated them.
Sweeping away the dust from the interior of the Malaya forest,
carrying off the abundant pollen of flowers,
and expert at absorbing the multitude of droplets from beads of perspiration—
The cool-scented breeze blew gently.
The King, beholding that wondrous miracle—
a great festival for the world such as had never been seen before— [was filled with joy].
With eyes wide open in supreme joy,
they performed a great worship with gems and other offerings. Then,
bearing upon his head even a mere fragment of the relics, he—
Having halted upon his excellent chariot, which was yoked with white horses,
covered with a spread of cloth, and adorned with a raised white parasol,
he entered Anurādhapura, the repository of auspicious signs.
In his own palace, which was adorned like the abode of the Lord of Devas,
the king of incomparable majesty sat upon a lion-throne spread with a woolen rug and a silken cloth.
The Lord of the Earth established the relics of the Sage within a costly relic-chamber,
having constructed it like the interior of a house and deposited the relics of the Lord of Sages therein, together with the sun-like parasol.
Desiring the bliss of the triple heaven, he worshipped them with various offerings day and night. And of those two—
the wife and the husband— each [was devoted] to the other.
Being pleased, Tisīhaḷinda bestowed many precious ornaments and other gifts,
and having given villages that served as residences for noble families, he performed acts of patronage.
The people of the countryside, the townsfolk, the city-dwellers, and others, having gathered together and being distressed at not seeing the relics of the Sugata,
praised the conduct of the Supreme One in the world.
They proclaimed this in the presence of the Lord of the Earth:
"The Lord of Dharma was born in the world for the welfare of the entire world;
he has acted for the benefit of all people."
The relic, which was distributed for the welfare of many people, we also wish to honor.
Having assembled the community of monks, the lord of the earth—
Near the city of Anurādhapura, in the Mārāmava residence,
the Teacher’s relic addressed that aspiration to the great multitude of people assembled for the purpose of worship.
There, amidst that great assembly of monks, there was one elder,
peerless in the power of his wisdom and dwelling in compassion;
thus [spoke] the great-minded Tisīhaḷapati.
He informed [the King], who was skilled in acting for the welfare of the world:
"Whoever acts for the benefit of those who depend upon him,
he becomes one whose conduct follows the true nature of the great."
Having brought out a relic during the spring season,
show it to the people who long for the merit [of such an act].
Having heard the well-spoken words of that self-controlled sage, [the king acted accordingly].
That best of men questioned the Saṅgha of monks once more:
"What place here could be more delightful for this great multitude to pay homage to the Relic?"
Then all those monks dwelling in their respective Nikāyas respectfully described their own respective positions;
and while their words were mutually conflicting, the King—
He neither welcomed nor rejected any word.
However, with a mind characterized by equanimity,
the king spoke again in the midst of the assembly of monks:
"The relic of the Lord of Sages will itself go in an instant to a place worthy of it.
Then the king, having returned to his own palace, [acted accordingly].
To those people who were longing for the naming of the relic chamber,
he prepared the city and the road to the monastery,
causing the lotus-forests of their faces to quickly blossom.
The streets, their dust settled by the sprinkling of water,
were then as delightful as beds of sand; banners,
variegated with gold and other ornaments, were raised aloft.
And the archways were inlaid with the forms of tigers and other creatures;
their shadows blocked the brilliance of the sun,
while rows of banners shaken by the wind seemed to display a dance.
The rows of trees along the road were of a uniform color, like a line of forest groves,
having grown into beautiful plantain-tree avenues;
and full water-pots, placed at intervals, indicated the presence of the virtuous.
"The desired happiness of heaven and liberation shall be attained";
thus, through incenses produced from *kappūra*, *sāra*, *tagara*,
and *agaru*, both foul weather and fair weather became auspicious.
Hanging nets of pearls and jasmine,
various pavilions were prepared,
and fragrant flower garlands were arranged there.
Resounding with the humming of swarms of bees greedy for the fragrance,
some departed adorned in the festive attire of their choice, while others carried handfuls of flowers filling their caskets.
Other people were carrying loads of fragrant powder,
while others there bore various great palm-leaf fans.
Then the Lord of Laṅkā, yoked with horses as white as the moon—
When the excellent chariot was illuminated by the radiance of jewels,
he established the relic of the Ornament of the Three Worlds and,
preceded by a prostration, spoke these words:
O Supreme Sage, as you went to the seat of enlightenment for full awakening,
and to the Gaṇḍamba tree to crush the heretics,
so today you have come to the Deer Park to distribute the Dhamma.
"Go yourself to the place suitable for the worship.
Then the king, skilled in appropriate conduct,
dispatched him with Phussa as the charioteer standing at the chariot.
Afterwards, he himself went together with a great assembly,
performing incomparable and extraordinary acts of worship.
Amidst the clamor of shouts and cries from the multitude,
With the neighing of horses spreading far and wide,
the great clamor of kettledrums, and the trumpeting of elephants,
the city became like an overflowing ocean.
The noble women dwelling in both rows, filled with joy,
cast their golden ornaments from the windows;
they rained down a universal shower of flowers everywhere.
The attendants themselves carried him on their shoulders.
When that chariot had reached the vicinity of the eastern gate, it was like a ship upon the surface of the ocean.
The throngs of ascetics and all the people there were delighted,
and they honored him with various offerings. Then,
having circumambulated him clockwise, they departed toward the north of the city.
Having exited through the gate,
that excellent chariot stood still at the spot where Mahinda had delivered his discourse on the Buddha’s Dhamma, like a merchant ship that has reached its destination.
At that place, the Lord of Laṅkā brought forth from the interior of a casket filled with jewels the supreme tooth-relic of the Conqueror,
like the evening clouds bringing out the moon.
He appeared before the people of the countryside, the merchants, and the citizens.
As that multitude was suddenly showered with rain— namely,
ornaments and other gifts— and was filled to overflowing with intense joy;
While the quarters of the sky were filled with the resonant sounds of the auspicious songs sung by the bards of Ānanda,
and while the lotus-like hands of the great multitude were raised;
And at the rising of the moon, when the lotuses had closed their buds,
amidst the immeasurable cries of "Well done! uttered by Brahmās,
gods, and others, as he spread across the sky and the interior of the world.
The teeth and the hair on the head were of an identical color, white as jasmine, fresh sandalwood,
and the rays [of light] from them— white as jasmine, fresh sandalwood, and the moon—
[illuminated] the palaces, gate-towers, mountain masses, trees, and so forth.
In an instant, he made it as if polished from silver.
Having seen that inconceivable miracle, which was most terrifying to mortals,
who here did not stand with their hair standing on end?
Who indeed returned their own ornaments to their homes?
Who did not disparage their own acquisition of self?
And who abandoned the stains of their own views with which they were bound?
Who indeed did not aspire to the greatness of the Buddha? Who, alas,
fell under the snare of stinginess and failed to go for refuge to the Triple Gem?
King Laṅkā also, having honored the incomparable relic of the Omniscient One with a retinue of nine hundred thousand [pieces of gold],
further enlarged that temple of the tooth relic.
In the inner palace, he passed away day after day.
Having brought the relic to the monastery for the great festival,
he performed such worship as this every year.
Then that king, named Kittisirimegha, who was true to his word,
had this charter inscribed upon a copper plate;
and others, too, caused this charter to be circulated.
Those lords of the earth, headed by Buddhadāsa—
delightful with the ornaments of virtues such as faith and compassion—
honored that tooth-relic of the Jina in many ways.
Having faith in the Teacher who, in a previous existence, was fully aware and discerning for the sake of what was to be attained;
having realized his Perfect Enlightenment which brings about the departure of all taints;
and having applied the ear to his supreme Dhamma, O one of subtle intelligence, meeting with the assembly of the virtuous at every gathering—
One should desire Nibbāna as peace, for the purpose of abandoning the fear of the three realms of existence and grasping it.
The fifth chapter.
This was composed by Candagomi in this excellent treatise on grammar.
And he composed a praiseworthy commentary on the *Pañcikā*;
furthermore, he produced a commentary on the *Pāsādikā*, the sub-commentary on the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*. He brought joy to the people through his radiance as a Buddha.
He composed a commentary on the *Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathā*,
which dispels confusion, delusion, and obstacles,
for the benefit of the community of self-restrained ascetics striving in meditation.
He composed the work named *Vinayasaṅgaha*—
to him who was devoted to the practice of those with tranquil faculties,
who delighted in the life of effacement, and who was ever concentrated.
To him who is adorned with the possession of virtues such as fewness of desires,
who is the cause of the great flourishing of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s dispensation,
and who has attained the highest status as a teacher among all—
To the Great Lord, who is skilled in all the various systems of the scriptures,
whose son was raised by his disciples,
and who is born of a pure lineage through the arising of virtues such as compassion.
By the one who is skilled and confident in logic, scripture,
and the rest, who is encompassed by the widespread mass of rays from the moon of his pure fame,
and who is renowned for his extensive splendor.
This tooth-relic of the Conqueror, which produces clarity of hearing,
belongs to the one named Dhammakitti— who was gentle through the wealth of faith,
honored by kings, and whose conduct was such— [and it was] by him [that it was brought].
The lineage has been made a lamp for the radiance of those who see all things.
May the Dhamma of the Lord of Sages endure for a long time,
and may the lords of the earth remain established in the Dhamma.
May the clouds rain in due season,
and may all beings likewise obtain the happiness of mutual friendship.
